findings.title: Malicious PowerShell reads LSASS memory with full-access handle on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, a PowerShell process (PID 2976) launched by control.exe with a hidden window and an obfuscated bitmap-decoded IEX payload opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (full-access, dump-capable masks) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z. Windows Security event 4663 corroborates the same process (user pbeesly, logon 0x372E81) accessing lsass.exe with 'Read from process memory'. This is consistent with LSASS credential dumping by the APT29-style PowerShell framework (which also ran keystroke logging, screen capture and exfil functions).

findings.title: OS credential dumping activity via LSASS handle from malicious PowerShell
findings.summary: The overarching OS Credential Dumping activity is present on scranton.dmevals.local: the compromised PowerShell loader (PID 2976, spawned by control.exe with hidden window and obfuscated payload) requested full-access handles to lsass.exe (0x1f3fff, 0x1fffff) and Security 4663 recorded 'Read from process memory' on lsass.exe by user pbeesly. No other credential-store dumping (SAM/NTDS/LSA secrets/DCSync) was observed.

findings.title: No SAM/SECURITY registry hive dumping observed
findings.summary: No evidence of SAM or SECURITY hive dumping: no reg save / SAM / SECURITY command lines in process creation (4688) or Sysmon event 2, and no 4663 object access to SAM/SECURITY registry keys. The only registry-key object accesses (4663) were generic 'Key' objects, not credential hives.

findings.title: No NTDS.dit / volume shadow copy activity observed
findings.summary: No NTDS.dit access, ntdsutil, vssadmin or shadow-copy activity was found in Sysmon file-create (event 11), Sysmon event 2, Security 4688 process creation, or PowerShell 4104 script blocks. No domain-controller credential database dumping is present in the data.

findings.title: LSA Secrets access is routine LOCAL SERVICE machine-account query
findings.summary: The 4662 events reading Object Server LSA, Object Type SecretObject, Object Name Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC with Access Mask 0x2 ('Query secret value') are performed by the built-in NT AUTHORITY\LOCAL SERVICE account (S-1-5-19) on nashua, scranton and utica. This is normal machine-account secret access, not adversary LSA-secret dumping; no lsadump/secrets command lines or 4663/4656 accesses to SECURITY\Policy\Secrets were seen.

findings.title: No cached domain credential (DCC2) dumping observed
findings.summary: No 4663/4656 object access to SECURITY or Cache registry keys and no PowerShell 4104 script blocks referencing cache/dcc2/mimikatz were found. No cached domain credential theft is present in the data.

findings.title: No DCSync / directory replication activity observed
findings.summary: No Security event 4929 (directory service replication) exists, and no process creation or PowerShell script blocks referencing drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync/Get-ADReplAccount were found. The single 4662 DS object access (newyork, NEWYORK$ machine account, Control Access) is not a replication request. No DCSync is present.

findings.title: netsh trace capture on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Network Watcher agent activity, not adversary sniffing
findings.summary: The only packet-capture-looking activity in the environment is `netsh.exe trace start capture=yes` (and the matching `trace stop`) on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z / 03:19:24Z. Both invocations were spawned by the Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (parent image C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service) running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, writing to a TEMP .etl file. The netsh.exe binary is the Microsoft-signed system binary (Company: Microsoft Corporation, OriginalFileName: netsh.exe, FileVersion 10.0.18362.1). This is the documented Azure Network Watcher packet-capture feature, not an adversary capturing traffic. The same two events appear in windows.security 4688 with the same parent. No Npcap/WinPcap/dumpcap/Wireshark binaries, drivers, files or registry keys were found anywhere in sysmon or security.

findings.title: No packet-capture driver or sniffing tooling installed; 7045 services are PsExec and a Java service
findings.summary: The five service-install (7045) events in windows.other are four PSEXESVC installs on nashua.dmevals.local (ImagePath %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, demand start, user pbeesly) and one 'Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service' on scranton.dmevals.local (C:\Windows\System32\javamtsup.exe, auto start, user pbeesly). None is a packet-capture driver such as Npcap/WinPcap/NPF. A targeted search for npcap/winpcap/dumpcap/Wireshark in process command lines, file paths and registry paths returned zero hits, and a search for pcap/sniff/promisc in security process command lines and service names returned zero hits. No evidence of a sniffer being installed or run.

findings.title: Zeek capture window shows no sniffing-related or anomalous protocol activity
findings.summary: The zeek dataset (2020-04-30, a window that does not overlap the Windows host data) contains only normal protocol logs: conn, files, ssl, x509, dce_rpc, http, dns, kerberos, smb_files, smb_mapping, dpd, weird, notice and pe. The 12 'weird' and 2 'notice' events are SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert (self-signed certificate) notices and generic protocol anomalies, none indicating packet capture or promiscuous-mode sniffing. No sniffing tooling or capture artifacts are visible in this window.

findings.title: PowerShell and wsmprovhost open LSASS with full access (credential API access) on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran a PowerShell credential-access toolkit (script path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) that included Invoke-Discovery and Get-PrivateKeys (exporting certificate private keys with password 'saribas'). At 03:05:16 PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, including 'Read from process memory'), and the corresponding Security 4656 handle request confirms AccessMask 0x1f3fff against \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. On nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29, wsmprovhost.exe (remote PowerShell, PID 0x1e28) as pbeesly requested AccessMask 0x1f3fff on lsass.exe. This is direct API-level access to LSASS credential memory, consistent with credential API hooking/dumping rather than normal system behaviour.

findings.title: No keylogging evidence found
findings.summary: Searches for keylogging indicators were negative: no PowerShell script blocks referencing GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx/RegisterHotKey/keylog (C069 zero hits), no keyboard/hook registry keys beyond default Windows keyboard-layout and device-enumeration entries (C066), and no keylogger service installed (7045 services were only PSEXESVC and Java Virtual Machine Support Service, C068). The keyboard-related registry writes observed are standard Windows CTF/KeyboardLayout and TERMINPUT_BUS device entries, not attacker keylogging.

findings.title: No GUI input capture / fake credential prompt evidence
findings.summary: The only process creations referencing credential/prompt/consent were three legitimate C:\Windows\System32\consent.exe executions (C071), which is the standard Windows UAC consent UI, not a spoofed credential prompt. No fake credential-prompt executables were observed among 4688 process creations (C073). The PowerShell script blocks matching 'credential' were benign Microsoft module resource strings (MSFT_ScriptResourceStrings.psd1) and the Get-PrivateKeys function, not GUI input capture.

findings.summary: No web-portal credential capture was observed. findings.title: Input capture family: LSASS credential access dominates; no keylogging/GUI/web capture
findings.summary: Across the T1056 family, the only malicious input/credential-capture activity is API-level access to LSASS credential memory (T1056.004) by pbeesly via PowerShell on scranton and via wsmprovhost on nashua, alongside a PowerShell credential toolkit (Invoke-Discovery, Get-PrivateKeys exporting cert private keys). The high-volume Sysmon 10 process-access events are otherwise dominated by benign svchost.exe/backgroundTaskHost.exe/Explorer.EXE accesses with GrantedAccess 0x1000, and the 4656/4663 object accesses are dominated by routine registry reads (Session Manager\Environment, Control\Lsa, Winlogon). No keylogging, GUI input capture, or web portal capture was observed.

No MFA/smartcard interception artifacts; only legitimate Microsoft smartcard provider and OS credential-service registration
findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other on 2020-05-02 found no interception tooling. The only smartcard-related image load is the Microsoft-signed SmartcardCredentialProvider.dll loaded by LogonUI.exe on scranton.dmevals.local (Sysmon 7), which is the standard Windows smartcard credential provider. All registry writes touching 'Credential'/'Ngc' keys are routine service registration by services.exe/svchost.exe (CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc, NgcSvc, NgcCtnrSvc, CredentialGuard). The 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly authenticating to NASHUA via PsExec (lateral movement), not MFA interception. No fake credential provider, no interception DLL, no MFA-related process or file was observed.

findings.title: No forced-authentication (T1187) artifacts; SMB traffic is normal domain/GPO and PsExec lateral movement
findings.summary: Hunting for T1187 forced authentication across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and windows.powershell found no coercion artifacts. All outbound SMB (445/139) connections in windows.sysmon originate from process.executable 'System' (the kernel SMB client) to the domain controller 10.0.0.4 or link-local IPv6 fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429, consistent with normal domain/GPO traffic rather than an attacker-controlled SMB/WebDAV listener. Share access (5140/5145) is dominated by machine accounts (SCRANTON$, NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, UTICA$, WEC$) reading SYSVOL GPO paths, plus user pbeesly from 10.0.1.4 accessing ADMIN$/IPC$ with PSEXESVC.exe, svcctl and samr — that is PsExec-style lateral movement (T1021.002/T1569.002), not forced authentication. The only .lnk files created (Sysmon 11) are benign Explorer 'Recent' shortcuts and a hostui.lnk in the StartUp folder written by powershell.exe (persistence), not .scf/.searchconnector-ms/WebDAV coercion files. No WebDAV/NTLM coercion script blocks were found (check C135 returned zero hits).

findings.title: PowerShell and remote WMI host processes opened lsass with full access (credential dumping primitive) during APT29-style intrusion
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, in an intrusion using the pbeesly account and SeaDuke tooling, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16Z, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29Z. These full-access handles to lsass are the standard primitive for reading credential material from LSASS memory, matching the T1212 credential-access hypothesis. The activity is part of a broader APT29-style chain: a Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service installed via javamtsup.exe on scranton, PsExec/PSEXESVC service installs on nashua, and PowerShell script blocks Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA and Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA. The remaining lsass accesses (svchost.exe 0x1000, Azure AntimalwareConfig/Telemetry 0x1400, wininit/csrss at boot) are normal system behaviour.

findings.title: No web session cookie theft observed; browser accesses are benign shell/COM activity
findings.summary: Across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there is no evidence of web session cookie theft. Searches for browser cookie stores (Cookies, Login Data, WebCache, Local State, Network\Cookies) in file-creation (Sysmon 11), file-creation-time (Sysmon 2), process command lines (Sysmon 1) and PowerShell scriptblocks (4104) returned zero hits. The only browser process accesses (Sysmon 10) target MicrosoftEdge.exe / MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe from C:\windows\Explorer.EXE and C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe with low granted access (0x2000/0x3000), consistent with normal Windows shell/COM interaction rather than memory scraping of session cookies. The genuine malicious activity on these hosts is a credential-access/lateral-movement campaign (PsExec64 with a cleartext password to \\NASHUA launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, plus sdelete64 cleanup), which does not match T1539.

On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block (Event 4104, ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) defining function Get-PrivateKeys. It enumerates every certificate in cert:\LocalMachine recursively and exports each one with Export-PfxCertificate to a randomly named .pfx in the user's Downloads folder, protected by the hardcoded password "saribas". A matching Sysmon file-creation event confirms the exported key material: C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe at 2020-05-02T03:04:57Z. This is direct theft of private keys/certificates from the local machine store.
findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys harvests all machine certificates to .pfx files

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly repeatedly invoked PsExec64.exe with the account password supplied in cleartext on the command line: "C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\PsExec64.exe" -accepteula \\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. Four such executions were observed between 2020-05-02T03:11:18Z and 03:14:42Z, targeting host NASHUA and launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. The credential is stored in the process command line (recoverable from process listings/logs), matching unsecured credentials in files/command lines. Corroborating PowerShell script blocks on the same host (Invoke-Exfil) also embed a plaintext password ("MyCozyPassw0rd!") for a WebDAV share.
findings.title: Plaintext credentials embedded in PsExec command lines used for lateral movement

LSASS handle access with full access rights by PowerShell/WinRM — credential dumping, not auth-process modification
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, WinRM remote PowerShell, parent svchost.exe) on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29. The wsmprovhost call trace runs through Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. a PowerShell cmdlet driving the LSASS access. This is credential theft from LSASS memory (T1003.001), not modification of the authentication process. The same user pbeesly was seen authenticating to nashua via WinRM/PSEXESVC and running an Invoke-Exfil script on scranton, consistent with an active intrusion. No T1556 modification artifacts (LSA registry, password filter, reversible encryption) were found.

findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (user DMEVALS\pbeesly) was launched by C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe and made 348 outbound TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443 (source 10.0.1.6), a non-standard port consistent with an SMB-relay/name-resolution-poisoning listener. A single NTLM network logon (4624, LogonType 3, LogonProcessName NtLmSsp, NTLM V2) for pbeesly was recorded on scranton.dmevals.local from 172.18.39.2. Zeek shows SMB (445) and NBT-NS (137/138) traffic in the environment. Together these are consistent with T1557.001 relay/poisoning activity, though the Zeek window does not overlap the Windows window.
findings.title: Python relay/listener tooling on nashua connecting to 192.168.0.4:8443, plus NTLM network logon

findings.summary: In the Zeek window, responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc appears for 559 of 613 conn records, answering for many different destination IPs (e.g. 10.0.1.6:55121, 10.0.0.4:123). A single MAC answering for the bulk of connections could reflect L2 redirection/ARP manipulation, but the MAC is a synthetic placeholder value and no Windows-side ARP cache or network-configuration evidence corroborates it; the Zeek window does not overlap the Windows datasets. Insufficient to confirm ARP cache poisoning.

findings.summary: No DHCP traffic (UDP 67/68) was found in Zeek or Windows security 5156 events, no DHCP server events (1341/1342/1020/1063) in windows.other, and no DHCP/netsh-interface command lines in PowerShell. No evidence of DHCP spoofing in any dataset.
findings.title: No DHCP spoofing activity observed

findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and zeek there is no evidence of Kerberos ticket theft or forgery. All TGS/AS ticket requests in windows.security (4769/4768) and all Zeek kerberos records use AES256 (0x12 / aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96) only, with no RC4 (0x17) downgrade, no anomalous SPN enumeration and no AS-REQ without preauth. The 4672 special-privilege logons are all normal machine/system accounts (NEWYORK$, SYSTEM, pbeesly, SCRANTON$). The only credential-access activity found is LSASS process-memory access by PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, which is credential dumping (T1003), not a T1558 technique.
findings.title: No Kerberos ticket theft/forgery observed; credential access present is LSASS memory dumping (T1003)

findings.summary: Golden ticket forging would show RC4 (0x17) TGS requests and/or special-privilege (4672) logons for accounts that should not hold them. All 28 4769 events use TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) for pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL only, and the 212 4672 events are all for legitimate machine/system accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SYSTEM 59, pbeesly 19, SCRANTON$ 4, DWM-1/2, NASHUA$, NETWORK SERVICE, LOCAL SERVICE). No forged-ticket indicators.
findings.title: No Golden Ticket activity: no RC4 TGS, no anomalous 4672 privilege logons

findings.summary: Silver ticket forging would produce service-ticket (4769) requests with RC4 encryption or for services/accounts not normally accessed. All 4769 events use AES256 (0x12) and target only pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL for services krbtgt, NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$ and WEC$ — normal machine/service account access. No RC4 service tickets and no anomalous service targets.
findings.title: No Silver Ticket activity observed

findings.summary: Kerberoasting requires requesting service tickets with weak RC4 (0x17) encryption to crack offline. Every 4769 TGS request in windows.security uses TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256), and every Zeek kerberos TGS record uses aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96. No RC4 service tickets and no SPN enumeration tooling (no setspn/GetUserSPNs/Rubeus/Invoke-Kerberoast in PowerShell command lines).
findings.title: No Kerberoasting: all service tickets AES256, no RC4 downgrade

findings.summary: AS-REP roasting requires accounts with Kerberos preauthentication disabled (PreAuthType 0). All 4768 AS-REQ events in windows.security have win.PreAuthType 2 (preauth enabled) for pbeesly and SCRANTON$, and all Zeek AS requests to krbtgt/DMEVALS.LOCAL use aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96. findings.title: No AS-REP Roasting: all AS-REQs have preauthentication enabled
No web-credential forging; only benign WebDAV cookie handling and PsExec credential use
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other there is no evidence of forged web credentials. The only cookie-related activity is the legitimate Windows WebDAV client: on scranton.dmevals.local, rundll32.exe running davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie for http://192.168.0.4/webdav, spawned by the WebClient service (svchost.exe -k LocalService -p -s WebClient) under user pbeesly. A single INetCookies file was created by svchost in a ServiceProfiles path (normal OS behavior). The lone PowerShell 4104 'cookie/token' hit is a benign Sysinternals readme.ps1 script (Get-AttributesMask). The 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe) lateral movement by pbeesly, i.e. credential use, not forging. No SAML/JWT/ADFS artifacts anywhere.

findings.title: Web cookie activity is legitimate WebDAV client and OS INetCookies, not forging
findings.summary: The only cookie-related events are the Windows WebDAV client setting an auth cookie (rundll32.exe davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie for http://192.168.0.4/webdav, parent svchost WebClient service) on scranton.dmevals.local as pbeesly, and a single INetCookies file created by svchost under a ServiceProfiles package path. No browser cookie theft, cookie-file tampering, or cookie-forging tooling was observed. The PowerShell 4104 hit matching 'cookie/session' is a benign Sysinternals readme.ps1 script.

findings.title: No SAML token forging artifacts observed
findings.summary: No SAML/Assertion/ADFS/JWT artifacts were found in any dataset. Searches for SAML, Assertion, NotOnOrAfter, ADFS, token and cert in PowerShell script blocks, windows.other messages, and sysmon process command lines returned zero hits. The zeek TLS server_name stack shows only 192.168.0.4 (no SSO/ADFS endpoint). No evidence of SAML token forging.

findings.title: No MFA request generation activity; authentication events are normal Windows/RDP logons
findings.summary: Hunting for T1621 (Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation) across windows.other, windows.powershell, windows.security and windows.sysmon found no MFA tooling, no repeated authentication-prompt generation, and no identity-provider abuse. The only authentication-related events are ordinary Windows behaviour: an RDP logon by user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local (TerminalServices events 1149/21 from source 172.18.39.2), an NTLM-in-use informational event (6038), and a Credential Guard configuration event (14). PowerShell 4104 script blocks matching auth keywords are all benign Microsoft module manifests (DSC xStorage, Operation.Validation, 7-Zip). DNS/network activity to login.live.com and Microsoft/Azure CDN IPs originates from svchost.exe, backgroundTaskHost.exe and BackgroundTransferHost.exe (normal OS telemetry). No 4625 failed logons and no MFA/authenticator/OTP processes or command lines were observed.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx files
findings.summary: On host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block defining function Get-PrivateKeys (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1). The function enumerates every certificate under cert:\LocalMachine recursively, and for each certificate with a Thumbprint calls Export-PfxCertificate to write a password-protected .pfx (password 'saribas') into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads with a random filename. This is direct theft of authentication certificates and their private keys. The export materialized on disk: Sysmon event 11 shows powershell.exe (PID 3876) creating C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 2020-05-02T03:04:57.460Z, matching the script's random-filename pattern. A follow-up script block Invoke-BeachCleanup (ScriptBlock ID 31f21f1d-9199-4d21-9ea8-...) deletes $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.pfx (along with *.bmp, *.png and %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z), consistent with anti-forensic cleanup of the stolen certificate material. The activity is attributed to the apt29-powershell hunt source and mordorDataset tags.

    Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.png" -Force

The remaining 4657 hits are wevtutil.exe (SCRANTON$) editing WMI Autologger EventLog-Application keys, unrelated to certificates. The Sysmon registry-set (event 13) hits under SystemCertificates/Cryptography are likewise routine certificate-store and CryptoAPI symbolic-link writes. None of these show an adversary exporting or forging authentication certificates.
